entries.sentence: The NHS says a missed period is the earliest sign of pregnancy, and a GP or midwife can be contacted once a test is positive.
entries.note: Missed period earliest and most reliable sign with regular cycle; contact GP or midwife on finding out.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a missed period is the earliest and most reliable sign of pregnancy for someone with a regular monthly cycle.
entries.note: Missed period earliest/most reliable if regular monthly cycle.

entries.sentence: Most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period, according to the NHS.
entries.note: Most home tests can be used from first day of missed period.

entries.sentence: After finding out about a pregnancy, the NHS says to contact a GP or midwife, who help arrange the first appointment.
entries.note: Contact GP or midwife as soon as you know; they arrange first appointment.

entries.sentence: Many NHS trusts let people refer themselves for maternity care without seeing a GP first, though the process varies by area.
entries.note: Trust pages describe self-referral online forms; local details vary.

entries.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad, severe tummy pain or shoulder pain with feeling faint.
entries.note: 999/A&E for heavy bleeding soaking pad, severe tummy pain, shoulder pain, faint/dizzy.

entries.sentence: For lighter bleeding or milder pain, the NHS points to the maternity unit, a GP or NHS 111 the same day.
entries.note: Bleeding with mild/no pain: maternity unit; GP or 111 as soon as possible.

entries.sentence: The NHS says the earliest and most reliable sign of pregnancy is a missed period, for someone with a regular monthly cycle.
entries.note: Missed period earliest and most reliable if cycle regular.

entries.sentence: NHS inform notes that an irregular cycle can make a missed period harder to notice.
entries.note: NHS inform: irregular cycles make a missed period harder to notice.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists other signs, including feeling or being sick, unusual tiredness, tender breasts and needing to pass urine more often.
entries.note: Nausea/vomiting, tiredness, tender breasts, urinating more often listed.

entries.sentence: Constipation, a metallic taste in the mouth and a stronger sense of smell are also on the list.
entries.note: Constipation, metallic taste, heightened smell sensitivity listed.

entries.sentence: Some people have very light spotting or bleeding around the time a period is due.
entries.note: Light spotting/bleeding in first weeks, around when period due.

entries.sentence: The NHS says sickness can start as early as week 4 and can happen at any time of day.
entries.note: Nausea can start as early as 4 weeks and at any time of day (search summary; page not individually confirmed).

entries.sentence: Symptoms vary a lot between people, and some people notice no obvious signs at all.
entries.note: Symptoms vary; some women have no obvious signs.

entries.sentence: The NHS says most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period.
entries.note: Most home tests usable from first day of missed period.

entries.sentence: Someone who does not know when the next period is due can test at least 21 days after unprotected sex.
entries.note: If unsure when period due, test at least 21 days after unprotected sex.

entries.sentence: Some early tests work sooner, so the packaging or a pharmacist can say how soon a particular test can be used.
entries.note: Some early-detection tests work sooner; check packaging or ask pharmacist.

entries.sentence: Tests come in different formats, and the instructions in the box explain how each one works.
entries.note: Formats differ; follow instructions.

entries.sentence: An out-of-date test may give an inaccurate result, so the expiry date is worth checking.
entries.note: Check expiry; may give inaccurate results.

entries.sentence: The contraceptive pill and HRT do not affect a pregnancy test, though fertility medicines can contain the hormone hCG and may change the result.
entries.note: Pill and HRT will not affect accuracy; fertility medicines can contain hCG and may affect results.

entries.sentence: A positive result is very likely to be correct when the instructions were followed, while a negative result is less reliable.
entries.note: Positive very likely correct; negative less reliable.

entries.sentence: After a negative result, the NHS suggests waiting a few days and testing again.
entries.note: If negative and still think pregnant, wait a few days and retest.

entries.sentence: It says a GP can be contacted if a second test is negative but the period has not arrived.
entries.note: Speak to GP if negative after second test but no period.

entries.sentence: Some GP practices and sexual health clinics also offer pregnancy tests.
entries.note: Some GP practices may provide free test; sexual health clinics offer tests (trust page).

entries.sentence: The NHS says that once someone knows they are pregnant, they can get in touch with a GP or a midwife.
entries.note: Get in touch with GP or midwife as soon as you know.

entries.sentence: Either one can help arrange the first appointment, which is the booking appointment with a midwife.
entries.note: They help arrange first appointment (booking).

entries.sentence: The NHS says this appointment should happen before about 10 weeks of pregnancy, partly because some tests need to be done by then.
entries.note: Booking appointment before 10 weeks, partly because some tests must be done by then.

entries.sentence: For anyone past 10 weeks who has not yet seen a midwife, the NHS says to contact a GP or midwife as soon as possible.
entries.note: If past 10 weeks and not seen anyone, contact GP or midwife as soon as possible.

entries.sentence: The first appointment may be at home, in a hospital, at a GP surgery or at a children's centre, depending on the local service.
entries.note: Locations vary: home, hospital, GP surgery, Children's Centre.

entries.sentence: The NHS says screening tests are always optional, and it is a person's own choice whether to have them.
entries.note: Screening is always optional: your choice (returned alongside pregnancy test search; NHS screening page).

entries.sentence: Many NHS trusts let people refer themselves for pregnancy care without seeing a GP first.
entries.note: Trust pages describe self-referral via online form; summary: many trusts let you self-refer.

entries.sentence: Some trusts use an online form, and others use a phone number, so the process differs from area to area.
entries.note: Local details vary; some online forms.

entries.sentence: One trust says its form gives the team time to arrange a first appointment for between 8 and 10 weeks of pregnancy.
entries.note: Buckinghamshire: online self referral form as soon as possible gives time to arrange first appointment between 8 and 10 weeks.

entries.sentence: Another explains that after an online form, an appointment for an ultrasound scan comes first, with a separate call or letter to arrange the first meeting with a midwife.
entries.note: Worcestershire: appointment for ultrasound, separate contact by post or phone for midwife meeting.

entries.sentence: That call may appear as coming from an unknown number.
entries.note: Call may appear as from an 'unknown number'.

entries.sentence: Someone registered with a GP is usually told about the pregnancy by the midwife team after the first appointment.
entries.note: GP usually told after first midwife appointment (summary wording).

entries.sentence: A person without a GP can register with a local practice.
entries.note: If you don't have one, you can register with a local GP.

entries.sentence: The NHS separates problems that need an ambulance from those that need advice the same day.
entries.note: Page separates 999/A&E from same-day advice.

entries.sentence: It says to call 999 or go to A&E for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad soon after it is put on.
entries.note: Heavy bleeding soaking a pad: immediate treatment, 999/A&E.

entries.sentence: Severe tummy pain, shoulder pain, or feeling sick, faint or dizzy in pregnancy are also signs of needing immediate treatment.
entries.note: Severe tummy pain, shoulder pain, sick, faint, dizzy are signs you need immediate treatment.

entries.sentence: Sudden, intense tummy pain with feeling very dizzy, fainting or looking very pale can mean an ectopic pregnancy has ruptured, which the NHS treats as very serious.
entries.note: Sharp sudden intense pain, dizzy/fainting, pale: ruptured ectopic tube; very serious.

entries.sentence: For a possible pregnancy with a combination of a missed period, tummy pain low down on one side, vaginal bleeding or brown watery discharge, shoulder tip pain, or discomfort when peeing or pooing, the NHS says to contact a GP or call NHS 111.
entries.note: Combination of symptoms, even without positive test: contact GP or call NHS 111.

entries.sentence: The NHS says tummy pain that is severe, or does not ease after resting for 30 to 60 minutes, needs urgent attention.
entries.note: Stomach pain severe or not going away after rest 30-60 minutes needs urgent attention.

entries.sentence: The NHS says the ectopic pregnancy page describes symptoms that usually start around weeks 4 to 12, and that an ectopic pregnancy does not always cause symptoms.
entries.note: Ectopic symptoms usually start around weeks 4 to 12 and not always symptoms (search summary).

entries.sentence: Bleeding is the main sign of miscarriage, but other conditions can also cause it, so the NHS advises getting it checked.
entries.note: Bleeding main sign of miscarriage; other conditions can cause it; get checked.

entries.sentence: For bleeding, the NHS advises contacting a GP or maternity team, or calling NHS 111, as soon as possible.
entries.note: Contact GP or maternity team, or call NHS 111, as soon as possible.

entries.sentence: For bleeding with mild or no pain, the NHS says to call the maternity unit if there is a number.
entries.note: Bleeding with mild or no pain: call maternity unit if you have number.

entries.sentence: Early pregnancy units, usually based in hospitals, can help with problems such as spotting, light bleeding or mild tummy pain.
entries.note: EPUs can help with spotting, light bleeding, mild tummy pain; usually in hospitals.

entries.sentence: Whether someone can use one depends on the stage of pregnancy and where they live.
entries.note: Availability depends on stage and where you live.

entries.sentence: Several trusts accept self-referral only in particular cases, such as a previous ectopic pregnancy or repeated miscarriages, and others take referrals only from a professional.
entries.note: Trusts accept self-referral in specific cases (previous ectopic, recurrent miscarriage, molar); others no self-referrals (search summary).

entries.sentence: The NHS says a person who is unsure can call NHS 111 or the maternity unit.
entries.note: If unsure, call 111 or maternity unit (search summary).
